Cloud Harvesting on the Floating Isles of Aeralith

A fictional geography and science lesson

The Floating Isles of Aeralith are an imaginary chain of islands that drift high above a warm ocean. The islands have no rivers and almost no rain, so the islanders collect their drinking water directly from passing clouds. This lesson uses Aeralith to explain condensation, the dew point and why fog nets work.

1. Where does the water come from?

Warm air over the ocean holds a lot of invisible water vapour. As the air rises towards the isles it cools. When air cools to its dew point, the vapour can no longer stay as a gas and it condenses into tiny liquid droplets. Billions of these droplets together form a cloud or a fog bank.

2. How a fog net works

Islanders stretch fine mesh nets, called cloud sails, across the windward cliffs. When fog blows through a sail, droplets hit the threads and stick to them. Neighbouring droplets merge into bigger drops, which become heavy enough to run down the mesh into a gutter. A single large sail can collect around 200 litres of water on a foggy morning.

Key points:
- Condensation is the change from water vapour (a gas) to liquid water.
- The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins.
- Fog nets work best on windy, foggy mornings facing the ocean breeze.
- Nets do not create water; they only capture droplets that already exist in the fog.

3. A common misconception

Some visitors think the sails "pull" water out of dry air. That is not true. On clear, dry days the sails stay dry, because there are no droplets to catch. The nets only work when the air has already reached its dew point.

4. Life on the isles

The islanders store water in clay cisterns carved into the rock. Every family helps repair the sails after storms, and the harbour master, a fictional character named Captain Zoë Marrant, records how much water each sail collects in the isles' café ledger.

Review questions:
1. Explain in your own words what the dew point is.
2. Why do the cloud sails face the ocean breeze?
3. Why would a cloud sail collect no water on a clear, dry afternoon?

Aeralith, its people and this lesson are entirely fictional and were written as synthetic test material for Dito Learn.
